questions.question: In SRP, what should the server store per user (ignoring metadata like account status)?
options: The plaintext password P
A fast hash of the password H(P)
A salt s and verifier v = g^x mod N
Only a salt s (no password-derived value)
questions.explanation: SRP stores a salt and a verifier derived from the password, not the password itself and not a simple reusable password hash.

questions.question: What is the purpose of u = H(A || B) in SRP-6a?
options: It encrypts the password before sending it to the server
It mixes the client and server public values into the exponent so they can’t be combined independently
It is the client’s session key K
It is a long-term server secret
questions.explanation: u is a transcript-derived mixing scalar computed from A and B; it ties the exponent to the session’s public values.

questions.question: Which formula matches SRP’s password-to-exponent mapping x?
options: x = H(P)
x = H(A || B)
x = H(v)
questions.explanation: SRP derives x from the salt and H(I ":" P), binding the password guess to the username and salt.

questions.question: In SRP-6a, what is the verifier v used for?
options: It lets the server authenticate the client without storing P, by enabling the server’s computation of the shared secret S
It is sent by the client during login to prove knowledge of P
It replaces the need for a salt
It is an ephemeral secret that must be regenerated each login
questions.explanation: The server stores v and uses it with A, u, and b to compute S; the client never sends v during login.

questions.question: Why does SRP include key confirmation proofs (M1, M2) instead of stopping at K = H(S)?
options: Because without proofs, an active attacker can splice transcripts and neither side knows if the other derived the same K
Because K is always the same value across all logins
Because the server cannot compute S without M1
Because M1 encrypts A and B
questions.explanation: M1/M2 bind the session key to the full transcript and provide mutual confirmation that both sides derived the same K.

questions.question: Attack-themed: what can go wrong if a server fails to reject a client public value A where A mod N == 0?
options: Nothing; A is always safe because it’s public
The attacker can force the shared secret S to a known value (e.g., 0) and therefore predict K
The attacker learns the server’s long-term verifier v immediately
The attacker can compute the plaintext password P directly from A
questions.explanation: If A is not validated, the attacker can construct degenerate values that force a predictable session key, breaking authentication.

questions.question: Which implementation detail most often causes client/server SRP failures even when the math is “right”?
options: Using different encodings/padding when hashing integers into the transcript (e.g., PAD(A) and PAD(B))
Using too long a password
Using a salt longer than 16 bytes
Using a username that contains a colon
questions.explanation: SRP depends on canonical transcript hashing; mismatched integer-to-bytes padding/encoding makes u, M1, or k disagree.

questions.question: After a database leak (salt s and verifier v), which statement is most accurate?
options: The attacker cannot test password guesses offline because SRP prevents it
The attacker can test password guesses offline by recomputing v from a guessed password and comparing
The attacker can immediately compute the session key K for any future login without interaction
The attacker learns nothing useful because v is random
questions.explanation: Given s and v, an attacker can try guesses offline by recomputing x and v for each guess and checking for equality.
